title: Quantum
subtitle: A comprehensive guide to quantum physics, technology, applications and historical evolution

intro.text: A comprehensive guide to quantum physics, technology, applications and historical evolution
Prepared October 2026. Historical events are distinguished from industry forecasts; commercial claims are not treated as proven quantum advantage.

Quantum science studies physical systems for which classical descriptions fail, particularly at atomic, molecular and subatomic scales. Its consequences already power semiconductors, lasers, magnetic resonance imaging, atomic clocks, LEDs and many sensing technologies. The emerging “second quantum revolution” engineers coherent superposition, entanglement and measurement to build quantum computers, networks and precision sensors. These three technology families differ greatly in maturity, engineering requirements and market readiness.

Central distinction: quantum mechanics is established science; quantum computing at useful, fault-tolerant scale is an active engineering frontier. Quantum computers are not universally faster computers, and many projected industry use cases remain unverified.

blocks.text: Quantization
Some measurable quantities, notably bound-system energies, occur in discrete allowed levels. Planck introduced energy quanta to explain blackbody radiation; photons carry energy E = h f.
Wave–particle behavior
Light and matter display interference and localized detection. A quantum state encodes probability amplitudes; probabilities follow the Born rule, proportional to squared amplitude.
Superposition
A state may be a coherent combination of basis states, such as |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where |α|² + |β|² = 1. It does not mean a classical object is simply in two definite states.
Uncertainty and complementarity
Noncommuting observables cannot generally have simultaneously arbitrarily precise outcomes: ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2. This is not merely a limitation of instruments.
Entanglement

A joint state can possess correlations not reducible to independent states of its parts. Bell tests rule out broad classes of local hidden-variable explanations; entanglement does not enable faster-than-light messaging.
Measurement and decoherence
Measurement outcomes are probabilistic; interactions with uncontrolled environments destroy accessible phase coherence. Decoherence is a principal challenge for quantum processors and networks.
Tunneling
Quantum amplitudes can penetrate classically forbidden barriers, underlying scanning tunneling microscopy, some electronic devices and nuclear processes.
Spin and indistinguishability
Spin is intrinsic angular momentum. Fermions obey the Pauli exclusion principle, shaping atomic structure and electronic bands; bosons can occupy the same state.

blocks.text: Prerequisites: linear algebra (complex vectors, matrices, eigenvectors, tensor products), probability, calculus, differential equations, classical electromagnetism, introductory mechanics and Python. Advanced work adds group theory, statistical mechanics, solid-state physics and information theory.

blocks.text: A quantum computing system combines physical qubits, control pulses, calibration, readout, classical electronics, compiler/transpiler, runtime orchestration, error mitigation or correction, and application software. A typical workflow maps a problem into a quantum circuit or Hamiltonian, chooses an algorithm, transpiles to a native gate set and topology, executes many shots, and statistically analyzes results. Hybrid approaches delegate optimization, preprocessing and validation to classical machines.
Physical and logical qubits

Physical qubits are imperfect devices; a logical qubit encodes information across multiple physical qubits with syndrome measurements and decoding. Logical-qubit counts, error rates and logical operation quality matter more than headline physical-qubit counts.
Gate model
Single-qubit rotations and entangling gates form circuits; common gates include X, Y, Z, H, S, T, CNOT and controlled phase. Universality does not imply practical speedups.
Analog simulation and annealing
Analog simulators engineer Hamiltonians directly. Quantum annealers address energy-minimization formulations; claims of general optimization superiority require careful comparisons.
Noise and fault tolerance

Errors include relaxation, dephasing, leakage, crosstalk, calibration drift and measurement faults. Error mitigation reduces bias without full correction; fault tolerance seeks reliable long computations despite imperfect components.
Benchmarks
Assess circuit fidelity, logical error per cycle, connectivity, gate depth, runtime, resource overhead, energy cost and end-to-end accuracy against the best classical method.
Shor
Polynomial-time factoring and discrete logarithms on an adequately large fault-tolerant quantum computer; threatens RSA and widely deployed elliptic-curve public-key schemes.
Grover / amplitude amplification
Quadratic query improvement for unstructured search under suitable oracle assumptions; does not give an exponential speedup for arbitrary database queries.
Quantum phase estimation
A foundational component for eigenvalue estimation and some quantum chemistry and materials algorithms; precise implementations may demand deep circuits.
Hamiltonian simulation
Models time evolution of quantum systems; among the most physically motivated routes to advantage.
VQE
Hybrid variational eigensolver for approximate ground-state energies; sensitive to noise, optimization difficulties and classical competition.
QAOA
Alternating operator ansatz for combinatorial optimization; practical superiority is not established in general.
Quantum machine learning
Quantum kernels, variational circuits and quantum data models are active research; data loading, trainability and benchmarking constrain near-term value.
Quantum walks and amplitude estimation
Offer provable speedups for selected structured problems and estimation tasks, subject to access-model and implementation costs.

blocks.text: Quantum key distribution uses quantum-state preparation and measurement to detect some forms of interception under explicit trust and device assumptions. It still needs authenticated classical communication and practical security engineering. Quantum teleportation transfers a quantum state using shared entanglement and classical messages; it does not transport matter or communicate instantaneously. Quantum repeaters aim to overcome loss over long distances but are technologically demanding.

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is different from QKD: it uses conventional computers and mathematical algorithms designed to resist known quantum attacks. NIST finalized FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), 204 (ML-DSA) and 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024. Migration requires cryptographic inventories, prioritization of long-lived secrets, interoperability testing, protocol upgrades and crypto-agility. “Harvest now, decrypt later” motivates earlier action for data needing decades of confidentiality.

Sensors exploit atomic transitions, spin precession, interference, squeezed light or coherent ensembles to measure magnetic fields, acceleration, rotation, gravity, time and frequency. Examples include optically pumped magnetometers, NV-diamond sensors, atomic interferometers, SQUIDs and optical atomic clocks. Constraints include vibration, temperature, dynamic range, calibration, packaging and field robustness. Quantum-enhanced sensitivity must be assessed at system level, not only in laboratory noise floors.

Value chains include cryogenic equipment, vacuum and photonics components, microwave electronics, control systems, semiconductor fabrication, quantum hardware, middleware/compilers, cloud access, cybersecurity integration and domain applications. Customers should distinguish research partnerships, proof-of-concept contracts and repeatable production economics. For a purchase decision, demand reproducible benchmarks, full classical baselines, operating cost, maintenance, integration burden and a clearly defined success criterion.

Key adoption barriers: expensive infrastructure; scarce cross-disciplinary talent; calibration and reliability; lack of standard application benchmarks; data movement and encoding costs; intellectual-property and export controls; and hype around unverified speedups.

blocks.text: Project A — Bell experiment simulator
Implement Bell-state preparation, basis rotations, sampling and CHSH statistics; compare ideal and noisy results.
Project B — Quantum chemistry comparison
Compute a small molecular Hamiltonian, compare exact diagonalization, VQE and classical approximations; report total wall-clock and errors.
Project C — Error correction laboratory
Implement bit-flip and phase-flip codes, inject noise, decode syndromes and plot logical versus physical error.
Project D — Post-quantum migration audit
Inventory cryptographic dependencies in a sample web service, classify risk and propose a migration plan using NIST standards.
Project E — Quantum sensor concept
Model atomic magnetometry or interferometric inertial sensing, including noise sources, calibration and field requirements.
“A qubit tries every answer and reads them all out” — false: interference and measurement constrain accessible information.
“Quantum computers break all encryption” — false: impact depends on the cryptosystem, algorithm and machine resources.
“More physical qubits means a better computer” — false: fidelity, connectivity, logical performance and overhead matter.
“Quantum teleportation moves people” — false: it transfers quantum-state information under strict conditions.
“Every optimization problem will become easy” — unsupported; complexity and classical baselines remain essential.
“Quantum biology explains consciousness” — not an established conclusion; separate experimentally supported effects from speculation.
“Commercial roadmap equals scientific achievement” — false: forecasts need independent validation.
Amplitude
Complex coefficient whose squared magnitude contributes to measurement probability.
Bloch sphere
Geometric representation of pure single-qubit states.
Coherence
Preservation of phase relationships necessary for interference.
Decoherence
Loss of accessible coherence through environment interactions.
Entanglement
Nonseparable correlations in a composite quantum state.
Fidelity
Measure of agreement between actual and target quantum states or operations.
Hamiltonian
Operator governing energy and unitary time evolution.
Logical qubit
Error-protected encoded information unit built from physical resources.
NISQ
Noisy intermediate-scale quantum, a label for limited noisy processors.
QEC
Quantum error correction using redundant encoding and syndrome information.
QKD
Quantum key distribution.
PQC
Post-quantum cryptography, implemented on classical systems.
Shot
One circuit execution and measurement sample.
Transpilation
Mapping an abstract circuit to a hardware-native implementation.
Quantum advantage
Demonstrated benefit over a clearly specified strong classical baseline on a relevant task.
